# Evaluation: learned preference model versus stated preference

*Generated by `npm run calibrate`. Every number below is computed on held-out people the model never saw. Nothing was tuned on the test data.*

## Verdict

**The learned model beats the stated-preference baseline on held-out data. Mean gain in held-out label accuracy is +0.28 (95% interval +0.26 to +0.30); it won in 30 of 30 splits.**

The model recovered the sign of 9 of 9 features the latent function uses, with cosine similarity 0.873 between learned and true weights, and 1 spurious finding (a feature with no true effect whose interval excluded zero).

Read the result for what it is. The labels come from a function we wrote, and the model class (a linear utility over named features) matches the shape of that function. A good score here shows the pipeline works and the finding is recoverable; it does not show the method would work on a real person. The nonlinear stress test below removes the shape match.

## Setup

- Calibration pool: 10000 generated profiles from a separate seed, of which 439 pass Eric's hard rules (city excluded). The funnel runs on a different pool of 500.
- Each trial splits the pool by PERSON: 70% for training, 30% held out. Training labels compare only training people (600 comparisons); test labels compare only held-out people (300). No held-out person appears in any training comparison.
- Label noise: choices follow a logistic (Bradley-Terry) rule on the latent utility, so near-ties are close to coin flips; 5% of labels are pure coin flips; and a fixed per-person idiosyncratic term that no model can learn is added to the utility. Even the true function scores below 100% on its own labels.
- 30 independent trials (different splits, different label draws). Intervals are 95% intervals of the mean across trials.
- "True utility" is the latent function including the idiosyncratic term. The oracle row scores the latent function against its own noisy labels, which is the ceiling for any model.

| scorer | accuracy on held-out labels | agreement with true order, all held-out pairs | rank correlation with true utility | top-10% overlap with true top 10% |

| stated-preference-v1 (in the repo) | 0.506 (0.491 to 0.521) | 0.505 (0.495 to 0.514) | 0.012 (-0.015 to 0.040) | 0.082 (0.058 to 0.106) |
| stated-mobility-v1 (literal reading of the pitch) | 0.247 (0.239 to 0.255) | 0.167 (0.163 to 0.171) | -0.852 (-0.859 to -0.845) | 0.000 (0.000 to 0.000) |
| oracle: the latent function itself | 0.814 (0.807 to 0.821) | 1.000 (1.000 to 1.000) | 1.000 (1.000 to 1.000) | 1.000 (1.000 to 1.000) |

Chance is 0.500 for accuracy and agreement, 0 for rank correlation, and 0.100 for top-10% overlap.

### Paired difference, learned minus baseline

| comparator | metric | mean difference | 95% interval | learned wins |
|---|---|---:|---|---:|
| stated-preference-v1 (in the repo) | accuracy on held-out labels | +0.28 | +0.26 to +0.30 | 30 / 30 |
| stated-preference-v1 (in the repo) | agreement with true order, all held-out pairs | +0.38 | +0.37 to +0.39 | 30 / 30 |

| stated-preference-v1 (in the repo) | top-10% overlap with true top 10% | +0.61 | +0.57 to +0.65 | 30 / 30 |
| stated-mobility-v1 (literal reading of the pitch) | accuracy on held-out labels | +0.54 | +0.52 to +0.55 | 30 / 30 |
| stated-mobility-v1 (literal reading of the pitch) | agreement with true order, all held-out pairs | +0.72 | +0.71 to +0.72 | 30 / 30 |

| stated-mobility-v1 (literal reading of the pitch) | top-10% overlap with true top 10% | +0.69 | +0.66 to +0.72 | 30 / 30 |

The stated-preference baseline in the repo scores near chance because it cannot see work and roots at all: it ranks on shared interests, intent, language, activity and age fit, none of which the latent function cares about much. The literal-mobility comparator scores far BELOW chance, which is the divergence expressed as a number: ranking by what Eric says he wants puts the people he would pick near the bottom.

## Did the model recover the latent signal?

Latent weights are shown in the model's units (logits per standard deviation of each feature), so the columns are directly comparable. A learned interval that excludes the latent value is not a failure by itself: label noise and the correlation between the rooted features (a person with a studio also tends to stay put) move weight between neighbours.

| feature | group | true (latent) | learned | 90% interval (cluster bootstrap over people) | sign |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| years_in_city | life | +0.62 | +0.33 | +0.15 to +0.56 | ok |
| nights_away_per_month | life | -0.54 | -0.30 | -0.51 to -0.11 | ok |

| photo_doing_something_craft | visual | +0.00 | +0.00 | +0.00 to +0.00 | no true effect |

- Spurious findings by group: visual 1. About one in ten features with no true effect is expected to show an interval that excludes zero by chance at this level, more when features are correlated. The visual features are the least reliable part of the model: the library has 60 portraits, and because they are matched to profiles on declared gender and age, the calibration pool draws on only 21 distinct ones. A visual weight is estimated from at most that many distinct images, shared across many people, and a feature that none of them shows (for example a nature setting) gets no weight at all.
- Top five features by size, learned: work_needs_a_place, old_local_friendships, years_in_city, nights_away_per_month, physical_practice.
- Top five by size, true: years_in_city, nights_away_per_month, work_needs_a_place, physical_practice, job_tenure_years. Overlap: 4 of 5.
- Rank correlation between learned and true absolute weights across all features: 0.700.
- This table is the headline split (seed 1), the model shipped in `data/calibration/model.json`: trained on 600 labels over 307 people, scored on 132 held-out people.

## Stress test: a latent function the model cannot represent exactly

Same preference direction (rooted is better), different shape: saturating years in city, a tenure threshold, an interaction between having a practice and place-bound work, and a capped travel penalty. The model is unchanged and still linear.

| scorer | accuracy on held-out labels | agreement with true order, all held-out pairs | rank correlation with true utility | top-10% overlap with true top 10% |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| learned (pairwise logistic) | 0.791 (0.784 to 0.798) | 0.870 (0.866 to 0.874) | 0.908 (0.902 to 0.913) | 0.587 (0.543 to 0.631) |
| stated-preference-v1 (in the repo) | 0.499 (0.487 to 0.512) | 0.493 (0.484 to 0.502) | -0.021 (-0.048 to 0.007) | 0.069 (0.048 to 0.090) |
| stated-mobility-v1 (literal reading of the pitch) | 0.234 (0.226 to 0.243) | 0.160 (0.156 to 0.163) | -0.861 (-0.867 to -0.855) | 0.000 (0.000 to 0.000) |
| oracle: the latent function itself | 0.831 (0.826 to 0.837) | 1.000 (1.000 to 1.000) | 1.000 (1.000 to 1.000) | 1.000 (1.000 to 1.000) |

Learned minus baseline, held-out label accuracy: +0.29 (95% interval +0.28 to +0.31).

## Probability calibration

Does "70% sure he picks A" mean A wins about 70% of the time? Held-out labels pooled over all trials, grouped by the model's predicted probability that the first person is picked.

| predicted P(first picked) | labels | predicted mean | observed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.0 to 0.2 | 2129 | 0.091 | 0.086 |
| 0.2 to 0.4 | 1598 | 0.295 | 0.288 |
| 0.4 to 0.6 | 1468 | 0.498 | 0.505 |
| 0.6 to 0.8 | 1560 | 0.703 | 0.703 |
| 0.8 to 1.0 | 2245 | 0.907 | 0.919 |

Expected calibration error: 0.007. Log loss on held-out labels, headline split: learned 0.476 versus oracle 0.424 (lower is better; 0.693 is a coin flip).

## Where the model is confident and wrong

Of 2868 held-out labels where the model's margin was at least 2 logits (about 88% confident), 166 (6%) went the other way.

Largest misses on the headline split:

- The model expected **Hiliokom Quarryholt (bookshop owner, 16 years in Barcelona, 2 nights away a month, has a practice tied to a place)** to be picked (margin 4.1 logits). The label picked **Hezaetil Glassholt (software contractor, 0 years in Berlin, 13 nights away a month)**.
- The model expected **Kaeruzias Fenthorn (veterinarian, 4 years in Lisbon, 8 nights away a month)** to be picked (margin 2.7 logits). The label picked **Ronibas Glassmere (freelance translator, 3 years in Lisbon, 27 nights away a month)**.
- The model expected **Hikiokaen Sedgeholt (carpenter, 12 years in Lisbon, 1 night away a month, has a practice tied to a place)** to be picked (margin 2.5 logits). The label picked **Hugaetia Sedgeholt (ceramicist with a studio, 0 years in Madrid, 3 nights away a month)**.

A confident miss is not necessarily the model's mistake. Labels include coin flips and individual taste that no feature captures, and the model cannot tell those apart from signal. Each miss is a case a person can look at and overrule.

## Visual feature extraction

The scene features come from a local vision-language model asked only about the photograph. Agreement with what the image generator was ASKED to draw, over 60 portraits:

| feature | agree | rate |
|---|---:|---:|
| setting | 48 / 60 | 0.800 |
| activityKind | 46 / 60 | 0.767 |
| people | 59 / 60 | 0.983 |
| photoType | 51 / 60 | 0.850 |

The generator can drift from its prompt, so disagreement is not purely extractor error. The portraits are reused across profiles, so errors are shared by every profile that uses the same portrait.

## What this does not show

- That a real person has a revealed preference that contradicts their stated one. Eric is fictional; the contradiction is built in.
- That the method works on real labels, which are less tidy than a logistic choice rule.
- Anything about attractiveness. No feature measures it. The visual features describe photographs.
- That the 30% held-out people are representative of the 500 the funnel runs on. They come from the same generator, not the same pool.
